vignette:
Nikolai had been working late in his studio apartment one evening, finalizing frames for an animation deadline, when two men he had barely noticed in the hallway forced their way in and assaulted him. What stayed with him most was not only the fear in the room but the way his body had locked in place on the floor, one arm twisted under him, breath knocked thin and shallow while he tried not to make a sound. In the weeks afterward, he found that certain images could pull him straight back into that moment: the hiss and orange flare of fire on a stove burner or in a movie preview, the sight of needles, IV tubing, or other medical equipment in a clinic, and even reminders of victims in news stories or online posts. When those things appeared, he would immediately put on loud music or turn up the television to drown out the image, or tell himself it could have been worse and force himself not to get angry about what happened. Those reminders did not just unsettle him; they drove him straight into those routines of noise and distance, and the more often he had to do that, the more fixed his belief became that the world was dangerous and that people were not what they seemed. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place and that people were not what they seemed, and he felt as though his beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed. Each fresh reminder seemed to confirm that way of thinking, leaving him with the sense that his old assumptions had been shattered for good and that danger could surface anywhere.

The memories themselves were unlike ordinary recollection. When the assault came to mind, Nikolai said it felt more vivid than memories of everyday life, as if the scene had more texture and force than anything from his usual days at work. The more he lived with that vivid memory, the more ordinary sights started to feel like warnings, so that a hallway shadow, a figure moving too quickly, or a person’s sudden shift in posture could pull him straight back into alertness. When that vivid scene took hold, he would turn up the television, pull on music, or push down his anger, because he had learned that silence and stillness made the images harder to contain. He would also feel his body in the same position as when the frightening event occurred, as though his shoulders had seized up again and the pressure of the floor was back under him. Those moments of remembering made him look around with immediate alarm, and he became intensely afraid that someone might be coming for him again. He frequently checked behind him while walking home from his animation studio, especially at night after a long shift, and sudden movements by strangers on the sidewalk or in the lobby put him instantly on guard. That feeling of being under threat made him watch doorways, count exits, and keep scanning the people around him, because planning for escape felt like the only sensible thing to do. Once the memory surfaced, it carried an immediate sense that the danger was not over, only close at hand again, as if it had moved from the hallway assault into his body and stayed there. He always identified escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere, scanning exits in cafés, the subway, and even the small screening room where he reviewed work with colleagues. Once he had seen how quickly the attack had taken shape, he began to watch other people as though they might change without warning.

That watchfulness kept the event alive in a different way. The more he monitored the street, the more the memory seemed to return with bodily force, and the more often it did, the more he felt compelled to distract himself, shut down anger, and compare his suffering with what could have happened to someone else. Keeping the TV on or music blasting gave him short relief, but it also kept the experience from ever feeling fully processed, and the memory stayed close enough that it would return again with the same force. On bad evenings he would sit in his apartment with loud music blaring or the TV on for hours, telling himself his injuries had been minor compared with what others endured, while carefully refusing to let himself feel rage toward the men or toward the fact that he had not been able to stop them. Yet those efforts never left him settled for long. When the memories became especially vivid, they brought the same physical posture and helplessness back into his awareness, and that in turn sharpened his suspicion that danger could appear anywhere and that he had to keep looking over his shoulder. By then, he had started crossing streets to avoid groups of men, lingering near doors, and planning every route home around how quickly he could get out if someone moved too fast.

Over months, this pattern narrowed his life. He still went to work as an animator, but the studio had become another place where his vigilance never fully switched off, especially when coworkers moved suddenly behind him or when a project required him to review emergency or medical imagery for accuracy. Fire in an animated scene, even when it was only an effect on a screen, could set off the same surge of unease that sent him reaching for distraction and scanning his surroundings. He was increasingly isolated, single and living alone, and he noticed that his tiredness and irritability were less about the workload than about how much energy it took to keep the fear contained. He finally sought help when he realized he was spending more time checking exits and looking behind him than paying attention to his life, and he feared that if he did not understand what was happening, the memories would keep pulling him back into that position on the floor. What he hoped for was simple but urgent: to feel safe enough to walk home, work, and sleep without constantly bracing for the next sudden movement.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows triggers leading to distraction, loud music, TV, and scanning exits, but it does not clearly state within one paragraph that the triggers cause those maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: Reminders appear, and negative beliefs are described, but no paragraph explicitly links the reminders to the negative appraisals as a causal result.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The memory returns vividly, but the vignette does not clearly state that the memory causes the distraction, suppression of anger, or other coping behaviors in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Threat: Although remembering makes him alarmed and afraid, no paragraph directly states that the memory itself leads to an increased sense of threat or danger.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette describes reminders bringing back the assault memory, but it does not state that the memory generates or increases those reminders.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: The sense of danger is present, but no paragraph explicitly shows that this threat feeling drives his avoidance, checking, or distraction behaviors.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not clearly state that feeling threatened causes the traumatic memory to return.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The coping behaviors are described, but there is no paragraph showing that distraction, avoidance, or checking leads to the traumatic memory.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
